prompt: An audio callback processes 64 samples per call at a 48 kHz sample rate. How much time does it have to finish each call?

options.explanation: That is 48,000 / 64,000. Divide block size by sample rate, not the other way round scaled.

options.text: 64 ms
options.explanation: That treats each sample as 1 ms. At 48 kHz a sample lasts about 20.8 µs.
That is one sample period. The callback handles 64 of them at once.

workedExample:
```
budget = N / fs
       = 64 / 48000
       = 0.001333 s
       = 1.333 ms
```

The next block is due every 1.333 ms, so all work for this block must fit inside that.

prompt: Which of these is acceptable inside an audio callback?

options.text: Printing the current note to the USB serial console
options.explanation: Logging formats text and does I/O that can block when the buffer fills. Set a flag and print from the main loop.

options.text: Allocating a new voice object when a note starts
options.explanation: Allocation has unbounded time and can fail. Preallocate a fixed pool of voices at start-up.

options.text: Waiting on a mutex until the main loop finishes updating parameters
options.explanation: The callback may wait indefinitely; on a single core the main loop cannot even run while the callback holds the CPU.

options.text: Reading a preallocated parameter value and computing samples with a fixed amount of work
options.explanation: Correct. Bounded, non-blocking work on preallocated memory is exactly what the callback should do.

workedExample:
Apply the test to each: is its run time bounded and does it avoid waiting?

| Action | Bounded? | Waits? |
|---|---|---|
| Print | No | Maybe |
| Allocate | No | Maybe |
| Mutex | No | Yes |
| Read + compute | Yes | No |

Only the last passes.

prompt: What runs during the gaps between audio callbacks on a bare-metal MCU synth?

options.text: Nothing; the CPU sleeps until the next callback
options.explanation: It may idle if there is nothing to do, but the main loop runs whenever no interrupt is active.

options.text: The main (foreground) loop and any other lower-priority work, such as reading knobs, parsing MIDI and updating displays
options.explanation: Correct. The callback preempts the main loop; when it returns, the main loop resumes.

options.text: The operating system's scheduler
options.explanation: Bare-metal firmware has no OS scheduler; there is just the main loop and interrupts.

options.text: Another copy of the audio callback, in parallel
options.explanation: On a single-core MCU, one callback runs at a time, once per block.

workedExample:
```
main  ===   =====   ====
cb       ##      ##     ##
```

The DMA interrupt triggers the callback (##). Everything else (===) is the main loop: controls, MIDI, display, logging.

prompt: A Daisy Seed runs at 480 MHz with 48-sample blocks at 48 kHz. Your callback's measured maximum is 300,000 cycles. What is the worst-case CPU load?

options.explanation: That divides by a million cycles, as if the budget were about 2 ms.
That inverts the ratio (480,000 / 300,000).
That compares against the per-sample budget of 10,000 cycles, but the measurement covers a whole block.

workedExample:
```
block  = 48 / 48000 = 1 ms
budget = 480e6 * 0.001
       = 480000 cycles
load   = 300000 / 480000
       = 62.5 %
```

That leaves about 37.5% headroom at the measured worst case, before any library overhead outside your measurement.

prompt: A friend says: "My block is 48 samples at 48 kHz, so my synth's latency is 1 ms." What is wrong with this statement?

options.text: Nothing; latency equals block duration
options.explanation: Block duration is the processing budget. Other delays add to the path from key press to sound.

options.text: Latency is always exactly double the block size
options.explanation: Double buffering contributes about one block, but MIDI transmission, waiting for the block boundary and converter delays also add, so there is no fixed multiple.

options.text: 1 ms is the processing budget; end-to-end latency adds MIDI transmission, waiting for the next block, output buffering and converter filter delay, then the interface and DAW
options.explanation: Correct. The lesson's estimate for the synth's own part is about 3.4 ms worst case, before the audio interface.

options.text: Latency depends only on the CPU speed
options.explanation: A faster CPU does not shorten buffering or MIDI transmission time.

workedExample:
Add the parts for a MIDI-triggered note:

```
MIDI note-on      0.96 ms
wait for block    0-1.00 ms
queue (1 block)   1.00 ms
DAC filter        0.42 ms
worst case     ~  3.38 ms
```

Then the interface's input conversion and buffers, and Ableton's monitoring buffer if used. Measure the total with a loopback recording.

prompt: Why is calling `malloc` (or any general-purpose allocator) in the audio callback a problem? Select all that apply.

options.text: Its run time is not bounded: it may search free lists or call into the system
options.explanation: Correct. You cannot guarantee it finishes within the block budget.

options.text: It can fail when memory is exhausted or fragmented, leaving the callback without the object it needed
options.explanation: Correct. On a small MCU with a long-running instrument, fragmentation is a real risk.

options.text: It may take a lock shared with other code, so the callback could wait
options.explanation: Correct. Many allocators are protected by locks, which brings in all the problems of waiting.

options.text: The compiler refuses to compile malloc inside a function called from an interrupt
options.explanation: Compilers do not check this; it compiles fine and fails at runtime, which is why it is a discipline.

workedExample:
The callback needs a worst-case time. An allocator offers:

1. Variable time.
2. Possible failure.
3. Possible locking.

The fix is to preallocate at start-up: a fixed array of voices, fixed-size delay buffers, and a lock-free queue for events.

prompt: You toggle a GPIO high at the start of the callback and low at the end. On a scope the pulses repeat every 2.9 ms and are 0.8 ms wide, but about once a second one pulse is 3.1 ms wide. What does this tell you?

options.text: Average load is about 28% so everything is fine
options.explanation: The average hides the problem: one block overruns its 2.9 ms budget, which causes a click about once a second.

options.text: The scope is faulty because pulses should all be equal
options.explanation: Callback time depends on what the code does; variable widths are normal, and outliers are what you are looking for.

options.text: The block size is 128 at 44.1 kHz and the code is too slow on average
options.explanation: The period does match 128 at 44.1 kHz, but the average (0.8 ms) is fine. The issue is the occasional outlier.

options.text: Something occasionally takes far longer than usual and overruns the deadline; find the rare path (for example a voice steal, a buffer clear or a hidden I/O call)
options.explanation: Correct. 3.1 ms exceeds the 2.9 ms period, so that block is late. Worst case matters, not average.

workedExample:
```
period = 2.9 ms (128/44100)
typical width = 0.8 ms -> 28%
outlier width = 3.1 ms -> 107%
```

Anything above 100% is a missed deadline. Look for work that happens rarely: clearing a large delay line, a search through all voices, or a log statement that only fires on certain events.

prompt: Electro-Smith's "Avoiding callback noise" guide describes a tone in the audio output caused by current transients when a long callback exits. With 48-sample blocks at 48 kHz, at what frequency would you expect that tone?

options.text: 48 kHz
options.explanation: That is the sample rate. The transient happens once per callback, not once per sample.

options.text: 1 kHz
options.explanation: Correct. The callback runs 48,000 / 48 = 1,000 times a second, so the disturbance repeats at 1 kHz.

options.text: 24 kHz
options.explanation: That is what you would get with a 2-sample block, which is the guide's suggested fix.

options.text: 50 Hz
options.explanation: That is mains hum in the UK, a different problem with a different cause.

workedExample:
```
callback rate = fs / N
              = 48000 / 48
              = 1000 Hz
```

With N = 2 the rate becomes 24 kHz, above hearing, which is why the guide suggests it as the easiest workaround (layout and power filtering are the proper fixes).

prompt: In the Teensy Audio Library source, the I2S DMA interrupt calls `update_all()`, which only sets a software interrupt pending; the software interrupt (priority 208, where 255 is lowest) runs all audio objects. Why structure it this way?

options.text: To keep the high-priority DMA interrupt very short, while the long DSP work runs at a lower priority that other urgent interrupts can preempt
options.explanation: Correct. Data-moving and other time-critical interrupts stay responsive; the heavy update runs at low priority but still preempts the main loop.

options.text: Because DMA interrupts cannot call functions
options.explanation: ISRs can call functions; this is a design choice about priorities, not a limitation.

options.text: So the audio update runs in the main loop
options.explanation: A software interrupt is still an interrupt: it preempts the main loop, which is essential for meeting deadlines.

options.text: To make the audio update run twice per block
options.explanation: It runs once per block; the indirection changes priority, not frequency.

workedExample:
Two goals conflict: DMA servicing must be prompt, and DSP takes a long time.

1. The DMA ISR does minimal work, then pends the software IRQ.
2. When it exits, the software IRQ runs (it outranks the main loop).
3. Higher-priority interrupts (for example serial MIDI data) can still preempt the DSP.

The update still has to finish within the block period.

prompt: You report "max CPU load 55%" in your project log. Which caveats belong next to that figure? Select all that apply.

options.text: The test conditions (voices sounding, effects enabled, knobs moving), since load depends on what the synth is doing
options.explanation: Correct. A maximum measured with one idle voice says little about a full chord with effects.

options.text: Whether the measurement includes library overhead outside your callback (format conversion, interrupt entry)
options.explanation: Correct. A GPIO toggle around your code misses that work, so the true load is higher.

options.text: The build (optimisation level, memory placement), because code location and caching change timing
options.explanation: Correct. Moving code from SRAM to QSPI, or a debug build, can change timing significantly.

options.text: That 55% load guarantees no dropouts at any future firmware version
options.explanation: The figure only describes the build and conditions measured. Re-measure after significant changes.

workedExample:
A useful log entry:

```
max load 55% (CpuLoadMeter)
8 voices, delay on, 2 knobs
moving, -O2, code in SRAM,
48 @ 48 kHz, 2026-10-04
```

This makes the number reproducible and shows its limits.

prompt: You are tempted to drop the block size from 48 to 8 samples at 48 kHz to cut latency. Your callback's fixed per-call overhead is 15,000 cycles, and the per-sample DSP costs 6,000 cycles. The CPU runs at 480 MHz. Is the smaller block feasible?

options.text: Yes; load stays at 60% because per-sample cost is unchanged
options.explanation: That ignores the fixed per-call overhead, which is now paid six times as often.

options.text: No; any block under 32 samples is impossible on a Cortex-M7
options.explanation: There is no such universal rule; feasibility depends on the overhead and per-sample costs.

options.text: Yes; load drops because each callback does less work
options.explanation: Each call does less work, but there are six times as many calls per second.

options.text: Barely: load rises from about 63% to about 79%, because the fixed overhead is paid six times as often
options.explanation: Correct. The per-sample work is constant, but the per-call overhead now dominates more of each shorter budget.

workedExample:
```
N=48: budget 480000 cycles
 work = 15000 + 48*6000
      = 303000 -> 63%
N=8:  budget 80000 cycles
 work = 15000 + 8*6000
      = 63000 -> 79%
```

It still fits, but headroom shrinks from 37% to 21%. This is the trade-off Teensy's source comments describe: lower latency at the cost of more overhead.
